definition: In artificial intelligence, model-based reasoning refers to an inference method used in expert systems based on a model of the physical world.
details: With this approach, the main focus of application development is developing the model. Then at run time, an "engine" combines this model knowledge with observed data to derive conclusions such as a diagnosis or a prediction.

explainer.lead: An inference method for expert systems in which the core engineering effort goes into building a model of the physical world rather than encoding many separate rules. It matters because the same model can support many diagnoses and predictions from observed data.

tiers.eli5: Instead of memorising one answer for every situation, you build a little working model of how the thing behaves, then use what you see to work out what must be going on.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers spend most of development time constructing and validating the model, then run an engine at runtime that combines it with observed data to produce diagnoses or predictions. A pitfall is that model quality bounds everything: an incomplete or wrong model yields confidently wrong conclusions.
tiers.paperLevel: A runtime engine takes a model of the system plus observed data and derives conclusions such as a diagnosis or prediction; the limits come from the fidelity and completeness of the model.

explainer.example: A device model plus sensor readings are combined at runtime to infer which component has failed and what will happen next.

usedIn.name: Prediction
usedIn.detail: deriving outcomes from a world model
